definition.text: A measure of how the quantity demanded of one good responds to a change in the price of another good.

facts.text: A positive value means the goods are substitutes; a negative value means they are complements; zero means they are unrelated.
The cross elasticity of butter with respect to margarine is 0.81: a 1% rise in margarine's price raises butter demand by 0.81%.
Fuel and new cars are complements, so a rise in fuel prices lowers demand for cars.
Governments use cross elasticities between drinks when setting alcohol taxes and minimum prices to reduce harmful drinking.

definition.text: The quantity of a good that people are willing and able to buy at various prices over a given period.

facts.text: Demand is not the same as desire: it means both wanting something and being able to pay for it.
It is a flow, measured per unit of time, not a single purchase.
The most important influence is the good's own price: normally, the lower the price, the more people buy.
Demand also depends on the prices of complements and substitutes, income, tastes, expectations, population size, climate and government policy.
If consumers expect a price rise, they buy more now to avoid paying more later.
Goods with no substitutes, such as insulin, have nearly perfectly inelastic demand: price barely changes how much is bought.
E. F. Schumacher challenged the assumption that meeting demand is the purpose of economic activity, distinguishing wise demands for genuine needs from unwise ones.

definition.text: The demand facing one particular firm: the market demand left unmet by other firms at each price.

facts.text: It equals market demand minus the supply of the other firms at each price.
With many firms, each firm's demand is extremely elastic and nearly flat, though not perfectly flat as textbooks draw it.
